o1.biggest_strength: It correctly moves capacity away from decaying blog posts and toward comparison pages and near-page-one commercial pages, with trial-rate math tied to the data.
o1.biggest_mistake: It delays the cookie-banner rewrite to month 2 and undervalues it by treating it like a normal blog post, even though the query matches Maya’s high-intent objection.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Put the cookie-banner and cookie-free analytics rewrites into week one, add internal links from high-performing docs pages, and tighten the month 2/3 page list so all 12 slots are named or clearly conditional.

o2.biggest_strength: It uses the strongest signals well: comparison pages convert, blog traffic is the wrong goal, and docs can be used to pass qualified users into trials.
o2.biggest_mistake: It spends month 2 slots on a GA4 migration page and an agency page without search data, while pushing the high-impression cookie-free analytics page later than it should be.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Move the cookie-free and cookie-banner rewrites into the first week/month, make the forecast less ceiling-based, and replace unproven new pages with pages backed by Search Console demand.

reason: Both are strong and usable, but Output 1 is a bit tighter on the owner’s constraint: it stays closer to the data, shows cleaner working, and gives a more concrete operating plan. Output 2 has good ideas, especially docs links, but its priorities drift more into unproven new pages.
